parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: For a signal transmitted along an optic fibre, state what is meant by:
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the energy carried by light as it travels many km through glass - does the received signal stay as strong as the transmitted signal?
parts.proper_answer: Attenuation is the loss of signal power (amplitude or intensity) as the signal travels along the fibre.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the journey down the fibre**
Imagine sending a bright pulse of light in at one end. As it travels it is partly absorbed by the glass and partly scattered out sideways. So by the time you get to the far end, less power remains.

Step 2: **State the definition**
That progressive weakening is what we call attenuation - the loss of signal power, amplitude or intensity with distance.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about something extra that was not part of the original transmitted information but appears at the receiver.
Hint 2: Think about whether this extra disturbance is predictable and wanted, or random and unwanted, and how it combines with the real signal.
parts.proper_answer: Noise is an unwanted random signal that is superposed (added) on the transmitted signal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate wanted from unwanted**
The wanted part is the clean signal you sent. In any real system extra random fluctuations get picked up from thermal motion of electrons, interference from other circuits, cosmic effects and even from the amplifier itself.

Step 2: **Describe how it appears**
This unwanted random extra is called noise. It does not replace the signal, it adds on top of it, so the receiver sees wanted signal + noise superposed together. That degrades the quality and can cause errors in decoding.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The initial section of the transmission line for a signal from a telephone exchange is illustrated in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

At the exchange, the input signal to the transmission line has a power of $2.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{W}$.

After the signal has travelled a distance of $52 \text{km}$ along the transmission line, the power of the signal is $7.8 \times 10^{-16} \text{W}$. The signal is then amplified.
parts.text: Calculate the attenuation per unit length, in $\text{dB km}^{-1}$, in the transmission line.
hints: Hint 1: Start by listing the two powers: input power at the exchange and output power after 52 km, and recall that a ratio of powers in dB involves a logarithm.
Hint 2: Think how to turn the total change in dB over the whole 52 km length into a value per 1 km.
Hint 3: Check the order of the ratio so you get the magnitude of the loss as a positive number in $\text{dB km}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: Total attenuation $\approx 125\text{ dB}$ over 52 km, giving attenuation per unit length $= 2.4\text{ dB km}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the total loss in dB**
For power ratios we use decibels with a factor of 10. The power drops from $P_{in} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ W}$ to $P_{out} = 7.8 \times 10^{-16}\text{ W}$. The change in dB is: $$ \text{change} = 10 \lg\left(\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}\right) = 10 \lg\left(\frac{7.8 \times 10^{-16}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}}\right) $$ $$ = 10 \lg(3.12 \times 10^{-13}) \approx -125\text{ dB} $$ The minus sign just means a loss. The magnitude of attenuation is about $125\text{ dB}$.

Step 2: **Divide by length to get per km**
Attenuation per unit length spreads that total loss evenly over the distance $L = 52\text{ km}$: $$ \text{attenuation per unit length} = \frac{125\text{ dB}}{52\text{ km}} $$

Step 3: **Calculate the final value**
$$ \text{attenuation per unit length} \approx 2.4\text{ dB km}^{-1} $$ This is the loss in dB for every kilometre of line.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The gain of the amplifier is $115 \text{dB}$.

Calculate the power of the signal at the output of the amplifier.
hints: Hint 1: Identify the input power to the amplifier (the weakened $7.8 \times 10^{-16}\text{ W}$ signal) and recall how gain in dB links input and output powers.
Hint 2: Think how to undo the logarithm to solve for the unknown output power when the gain is 115 dB.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the gain equation**
Gain in dB for power is defined in the same way: $$ G_{\text{dB}} = 10 \lg\left(\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}\right) $$ Here $P_{in} = 7.8 \times 10^{-16}\text{ W}$ and $G_{\text{dB}} = 115\text{ dB}$, so: $$ 115 = 10 \lg\left(\frac{P_{out}}{7.8 \times 10^{-16}}\right) $$

Step 2: **Solve for the output power**
Divide by 10 and then use powers of 10 to undo the log: $$ \lg\left(\frac{P_{out}}{7.8 \times 10^{-16}}\right) = 11.5 $$ $$ \frac{P_{out}}{7.8 \times 10^{-16}} = 10^{11.5} $$ $$ P_{out} = 7.8 \times 10^{-16} \times 10^{11.5} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ W} $$ The amplifier boosts the tiny attenuated signal back up to a usable level.
